title: About
text:
I develop machine learning methods for medical image acquisition and analyses. Such methods aim to condense high-dimensional pixel arrays (images) into high-level semantic information that can aid diagnosis, treatment or clinical research. Furthermore, automated algorithms can also help improve image acquisition directly by reducing scan times or amount of radiation deposited to a patient, as well as by improving image quality.
To this end, my main research interests are two-fold. One, I particularly enjoy designing theoretically-grounded predictive algorithms that work robustly in clinical settings, while relying on only small-sized annotated datasets and respecting data privacy concerns. Two, I am interested in uncovering causal interactions in multivariate data, and in building statistical generative models for high-dimensional data understanding and manipulation.

title: Machine Learning Optimization Basics
text:
Training a neural network typically involves minimizing a loss function using gradient-based optimization. Here, let’s review the basic mathematical objects behind these algorithms: gradients, Jacobians and Hessians.






NoteSetup





Consider a model \(f_\theta\) trained via supervised learning to classify inputs \(x\) into \(k\) classes. The model produces logits \(z = f_\theta(x) \in \mathbb{R}^k\), which are converted into predicted class probabilities via the softmax function: \(\hat{y} = \sigma(z) \in \mathbb{R}^k\). The ground-truth label is represented as a one-hot vector \(y\). Training finds parameters that minimize a loss between predicted and ground-truth labels over a dataset: \(\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ell(y_n, \hat{y}_n)\).
Dimensions:

\(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\)
\(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}\)
\(z, \hat{y}, y \in \mathbb{R}^k\)
\(\ell: \mathbb{R}^k \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}\)











NoteGradients, Jacobians and Hessians





Solving the optimization requires understanding how the loss and model outputs change as parameters move through \(\mathbb{R}^p\). Three mathematical objects characterize this:

the Gradient \(\nabla_\theta \ell \in \mathbb{R}^p\) (first-order change of the (scalar) loss w.r.t. (vector) \(\theta\))
the Jacobian \(J_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times p}\) (first-order change of the (vector) logits w.r.t. (vector) \(\theta\))
the Hessian \(H_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}\) (second-order change of the (scalar) loss w.r.t. (vector) \(\theta\))


Gradient
The gradient \(\nabla_\theta \ell(y, f_\theta(x)) \in \mathbb{R}^p\) measures how the loss changes with each parameter. It points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss. Gradient descent steps in the opposite direction, where \(\eta\) is the learning rate:
\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \ell\]

Jacobian
The Jacobian \(J_\theta = \frac{\partial f_\theta(x)}{\partial \theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times p}\) captures how each output logit \(z_i\) changes with each parameter. It connects model outputs to parameters and is essential for computing gradients via the chain rule (Section 3):
\[J_\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial \theta_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial \theta_p} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial z_k}{\partial \theta_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial z_k}{\partial \theta_p} \end{bmatrix}\]
Its \(i\)-th row is \(\frac{\partial z_i}{\partial \theta} \in \mathbb{R}^p\), describing the sensitivity of class \(i\) to all parameters.

Hessian
The Hessian \(H_\theta = \nabla_\theta^2 \ell \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}\) measures the curvature of the loss landscape:
\[H_\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta_1^2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta_1 \partial \theta_p} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta_p \partial \theta_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta_p^2} \end{bmatrix}\]
Large eigenvalues of \(H_\theta\) indicate sharp curvature, while small eigenvalues indicate flat directions.










NoteBackpropagation as a Vector–Jacobian Product





Why the Jacobian matters
The Jacobian \(J_\theta\) is crucial in the computation of gradients via the chain rule, and is central to how neural networks are trained. Gradient descent requires \(\nabla_\theta \ell(y, f_\theta(x)) \in \mathbb{R}^p\), the gradient of the scalar loss w.r.t. model parameters. By the chain rule, this is a vector-Jacobian product (VJP):
\[\nabla_\theta \ell = \underbrace{(\nabla_z \ell)^\top}_{\mathbb{R}^{1\times k}} \underbrace{J_\theta}_{\mathbb{R}^{k\times p}} \in \mathbb{R}^p\]
where \(\nabla_z \ell \in \mathbb{R}^k\) is the gradient of the loss w.r.t. the logits.

Computing Gradients efficiently
Backpropagation computes this VJP efficiently by traversing the computation graph in reverse, accumulating gradients layer by layer without ever materializing \(J_\theta\). This costs \(O(p)\) and is achieved in a single backward pass, the same order as the forward pass.
The naive alternative would be to form \(J_\theta\) explicitly row by row and then multiply. This requires \(k\) backward passes at \(O(kp)\) compute, and storing the full \(k \times p\) matrix in memory. For modern networks where \(p\) can be in the billions, both the \(k\times\) compute overhead and the \(k \times p\) memory cost make explicit Jacobian materialization infeasible.










NoteHessian approximations in practice





This section motivates and derives the widely used Adam optimizer in three steps: (1) show why curvature matters, (2) approximate it cheaply using the diagonal Hessian, (3) see how Adam implements that.
Why the Hessian matters
Vanilla gradient descent uses the same learning rate for every parameter:
\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \ell\]
However, different directions in parameter space may have very different curvature. Ideally we would account for this using Newton’s method (see Appendix A):
\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H_\theta^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell\]
The inverse Hessian rescales the gradient: steps are larger in flat directions and smaller in steep ones. Unfortunately, \(H_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\) is far too large to compute or invert for modern networks.

Diagonal curvature approximation
A common simplification is to approximate only the diagonal of the Hessian. This gives a per-parameter learning rate, where \(h_i\) estimates the curvature of parameter \(i\):
\[\theta_{t+1,i} = \theta_{t,i} - \eta \, \frac{\nabla_{\theta_i}\ell}{\sqrt{h_i}}\]
For likelihood-based losses, the diagonal of the expected Hessian can be approximated using squared gradients (see Appendix B):
\[\text{diag}(\mathbb{E}[H_\theta]) \approx \mathbb{E}[(\nabla_\theta \ell)^2]\]
This makes curvature estimation possible using gradients alone!

Adam
Adam implements the diagonal curvature idea by maintaining two running estimates in parallel: one for direction (\(m_t\), the smoothed gradient) and one for scale (\(v_t\), the smoothed squared gradient):
\[
\nabla_\theta \ell \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{EMA}_{\beta_1}\;}\; \underset{\text{direction}}{m_t}
\qquad\qquad
(\nabla_\theta \ell)^2 \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{EMA}_{\beta_2}\;}\; \underset{\text{scale}}{v_t}
\]
\[m_t = \beta_1 m_{t-1} + (1-\beta_1)\nabla_\theta \ell, \qquad v_t = \beta_2 v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2)(\nabla_\theta \ell)^2\]
The two moments are then combined into the update:
\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \frac{m_t}{\sqrt{v_t}+\epsilon}\]
The denominator \(\sqrt{v_t}\) acts as a diagonal curvature estimate, scaling each parameter’s update by its historical gradient magnitude.










NoteAppendix A: Newton’s method from a Taylor expansion





The motivation for Newton’s update comes from minimizing a local quadratic approximation of the loss. Expanding \(\ell(\theta)\) around \(\theta_t\) via a second-order Taylor expansion: \(\ell(\theta) \approx \ell(\theta_t) + \nabla_\theta \ell^\top (\theta - \theta_t) + \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \theta_t)^\top H_\theta (\theta - \theta_t)\). Setting the derivative of this quadratic w.r.t. \(\theta\) to zero: \(\nabla_\theta \ell + H_\theta (\theta - \theta_t) = 0 \implies \theta = \theta_t - H_\theta^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell\). Thus, Newton’s update finds the exact minimum of the local quadratic approximation in one step, rather than just following the gradient with a fixed step size.









NoteAppendix B: Diagonal Hessian Approximation





For likelihood-based models, curvature can be approximated with squared gradients! Starting from the normalization condition, \(\int p(y|x,\theta)\, dy = 1\), and differentiating twice w.r.t. \(\theta\) (using the log-derivative trick \(\nabla_\theta p = p\,\nabla_\theta \log p\) at each step) yields: \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta^2 \log p] = - \mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla_\theta \log p)(\nabla_\theta \log p)^\top\right]\). If the training loss is the negative log-likelihood \(\ell = -\log p(y|x,\theta)\). Thus, \(\mathbb{E}[H_\theta] = \mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla_\theta \ell)(\nabla_\theta \ell)^\top\right]\). Taking the diagonal: \(\text{diag}(\mathbb{E}[H_\theta]) = \mathbb{E}[(\nabla_\theta \ell)^2]\). Thus, the expected squared gradient per parameter provides a practical estimate of the diagonal curvature.
Intuition
At first it may seem surprising that curvature (a second-order quantity) can be estimated using gradients (a first-order quantity). The key point is that the relationship holds in expectation over the dataset, rather than at individual datapoints.
Consider the gradient of the loss with respect to a parameter \(\theta_j\) for each training example: \(g_{i,j} = \frac{\partial \ell(x_i, y_i)}{\partial \theta_j}\). If the loss surface is strongly curved along parameter \(\theta_j\), the gradient with respect to that parameter changes rapidly as \(\theta_j\) varies, which manifests as large variability in per-sample gradients across the dataset.
Now, the expected squared gradient can be decomposed as \(\mathbb{E}[g_{i,j}^2] = (\mathbb{E}[g_{i,j}])^2 + \mathrm{Var}(g_{i,j})\), i.e. it captures both the average gradient signal and the variability of gradients across samples. Under the likelihood assumptions above, this second moment corresponds to the expected curvature along that parameter.
Caveats

Exact only for negative log-likelihood losses.
Uses the expected Hessian, not the local Hessian at \(\theta_t\).
Captures only diagonal curvature.

title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning in Vision
text:
A visual encoder learns to represent whatever its training objective rewards. Supervised training optimizes for a fixed label set: the resulting representations encode what distinguishes those labels, which may not be what a different task requires. Self-supervised learning (SSL) sidesteps labels entirely, learning representations directly from the structure of images. This note covers the three main SSL principles: contrastive learning, self-distillation, and masked prediction.






NoteMotivation





Supervised pretraining on large labelled datasets, followed by fine-tuning, works well when the target task resembles the pretraining labels. However, it has two structural limitations: (1) Labels are expensive. In domains like medical imaging, curating a large labelled dataset requires significant expert effort, while unlabelled data is far more accessible. (2), labels impose a particular partitioning of the visual world. A classifier trained on ImageNet learns representations shaped by ImageNet categories; those features may not be the most relevant for a different task. SSL optimizes no specific label set; it learns the general structure of the visual world.
SSL became the dominant pretraining paradigm for three reasons: (1) unlabelled data are abundant; (2) ViTs, lacking the inductive biases of CNNs, scale particularly well on diverse unlabelled data; and (3) the results are compelling. DINOv2 and DINOv3, trained on hundreds of millions of images, produce encoders that support diverse downstream tasks from a single frozen backbone.










NoteWhat Is a Good Representation?





A representation is a function \(f_\theta\) that maps an image \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}\) to a feature vector \(z \in \mathbb{R}^d\):
\[
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}}{x}
\;\xrightarrow{\;f_\theta\;}\;
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}\mathbb{R}^d}{z}
\]
A good \(z\) should capture the underlying factors of variation in an image (identity, pose, disease state, lighting) while discarding nuisance surface variation, as formalized in a seminal framework for representation learning. This motivates four concrete properties.
Semantic. Images with similar content should map to nearby points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). A chest X-ray with pneumonia should be closer to other pneumonia cases than to normal scans.
Invariant. The representation should be insensitive to changes that do not affect semantics: lighting, viewpoint, color, slight cropping. These are nuisance factors: they change pixels but not meaning.
Discriminative. Images with different semantic content should be far apart. Invariance alone is not enough; the trivial solution of mapping everything to zero is perfectly invariant but useless.
Transferable. The features should be reusable across tasks without being retrained from scratch. This favors general structure over task-specific detail.
These four properties define the target. The three SSL methods in Section 4 each pursue them from a different angle.










NoteThe Self-Supervised Setup





The core insight behind visual SSL is that a single image can be transformed in many ways that preserve its semantic content. A crop of a dog is still a dog. A color-jittered chest X-ray still shows the same anatomy.
Given an image \(x\), we sample two augmented views by drawing two stochastic transformations \(t_1, t_2\) from an augmentation distribution \(\mathcal{T}\):
\[
x_1 = t_1(x), \qquad x_2 = t_2(x), \qquad t_1, t_2 \sim \mathcal{T}
\]
Each \(t_i\) applies a random combination of operations such as random resized crop, horizontal flip, color jitter, grayscale, and Gaussian blur. We call \((x_1, x_2)\) a positive pair: same semantic content, different appearance. The learning signal comes entirely from this structure: a good encoder should map \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) to nearby representations. Images from different sources are negatives; their representations should be far apart.
The choice of augmentations defines what the encoder learns to be invariant to; random resized crops with large scale variation are the most critical choice, forcing the encoder to recognize content across different spatial extents rather than memorizing texture.










NoteThree Ways to Learn Without Labels





Given two semantically equivalent views \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), how should we define the learning objective? There are three dominant answers.







NoteA. Contrastive Learning





Idea. Compare against negatives: pull positive pairs together, push negatives apart.
Each view passes through the encoder \(f_\theta\) and a small projection head, producing a normalized embedding \(z_i\):
\[
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}}{x_i}
\;\xrightarrow{\;f_\theta\;}\;
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}\mathbb{R}^d}{h_i}
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{project + norm}\;}\;
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}\|\cdot\|=1}{z_i}
\]
The projection head is discarded after pretraining; \(h_i\) is the representation used downstream. The loss treats matching as classification: identify \(z_2\) as the positive among \(K-1\) negatives (InfoNCE, detailed in Appendix A):
\[
\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(z_1 \cdot z_2\, /\, \tau)}{\exp(z_1 \cdot z_2\, /\, \tau) \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \exp(z_1 \cdot z_k^-\, /\, \tau)}
\]
where \(\tau\) is temperature and \(z_k^-\) are negatives.
SimCLR uses all other images in a large batch as negatives, requiring batch sizes of 4096 or more. CLIP replaces augmented views with image-text pairs: the positive for each image is its caption, and all other captions are negatives. CLIP sidesteps augmentation design entirely and produces representations that support zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval.
Contrastive methods are effective but require many negatives. Self-distillation, described next, achieves competitive results without them.










NoteB. Self-Distillation





Idea. Train two networks to agree on their output distributions, where one network is a slowly-updating copy of the other.
The setup has two networks with the same architecture: a student with parameters \(\theta\) and a teacher with parameters \(\xi\). The teacher is not updated by gradient descent. Instead, its weights are an exponential moving average of the student’s weights:
\[
\xi \;\leftarrow\; \tau\,\xi \;+\; (1-\tau)\,\theta
\]
where \(\tau\) is a momentum coefficient close to 1 (e.g., 0.996). The teacher is always a slightly older, smoother version of the student.
Given two views \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), the student processes one view and the teacher the other. Both produce a distribution over \(K\) prototype dimensions via a softmax with temperature:
\[
p_s = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{f_\theta(x_1)}{\tau_s}\right),
\qquad
p_t = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{f_\xi(x_2) - c}{\tau_t}\right)
\]
The student is trained to match the teacher’s output by minimizing the cross-entropy \(H(p_t,\, p_s)\), with no gradient flowing through the teacher.
Without countermeasures, this system collapses: both networks converge to the same constant output for all inputs. DINO prevents this with centering (subtract a running mean \(c\) from the teacher output to prevent single-dimension dominance) and sharpening (lower teacher temperature \(\tau_t < \tau_s\) to keep the training target peaked); see Appendix A for details.
BYOL established that negatives are not needed: it uses an asymmetric prediction head on the student side only, alongside the EMA teacher, to prevent collapse.
DINO applies this framework to ViTs, using the CLS token as representation and multi-crop training (teacher sees a global crop; student sees multiple smaller local crops). A striking finding: DINO attention heads spontaneously segment semantically coherent regions with no segmentation supervision, discussed further in Section 5.










NoteC. Masked Prediction





Idea. Hide part of the input and train the model to predict what is missing.
MAE (Masked Autoencoders) applies this to ViTs by masking a large fraction of patches (typically 75%) and reconstructing the original pixel values.
The encoder processes only visible patches, so its cost scales with \(N_\text{vis} = (1-m) \cdot N\) rather than the full sequence:
\[
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}}{x}
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{patch + mask}\;}\;
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}N_\text{vis}\times d}{X_\text{vis}}
\;\xrightarrow{\;L\text{ blocks}\;}\;
\underset{\rule{0pt}{1.5ex}N_\text{vis}\times d}{Z_\text{vis}}
\]
A lightweight decoder then takes the encoder output alongside learnable mask tokens and reconstructs the pixel values of all \(N\) patches; the loss is MSE over the masked patches only.
The 75% mask ratio is critical. Low masking ratios allow reconstruction by interpolating from nearby visible patches, which does not require understanding object structure. A 75% mask forces the encoder to reason about global context to fill in large missing regions.
After pretraining, the decoder is discarded and the encoder is used as a feature extractor. MAE converges faster than DINO but produces somewhat weaker features for dense prediction tasks; DINOv2 combines both objectives to capture the benefits of each.













NoteWhy These Methods Work





The three methods enforce view consistency through different mechanisms, but the learned representations share two properties that go beyond what the training objective explicitly requires.
Object-centric structure. At no point during training does the model see segmentation labels, yet at convergence DINO’s CLS token attention maps highlight foreground objects and different heads attend to different semantic parts of the scene. This structure emerges from the requirement to match views of the same scene that differ in crop and appearance.
Geometry of the embedding space. Semantically related inputs cluster together, and representations spread uniformly across the hypersphere (see Appendix A for the alignment and uniformity decomposition).
Both properties have a direct consequence for transfer. SSL does not learn a classifier; it learns a representation space organized by semantic content. Fine-tuning on a labelled dataset finds boundaries within a structure that is already there. A linear probe works on many tasks because semantic consistency across views is what the training objective required, and semantic consistency is exactly what a linear classifier exploits.
All three methods optimize surrogate objectives (matching views, matching a teacher, reconstructing missing content), yet consistently recover semantic, object-centric representations that transfer across diverse downstream tasks. This is not a coincidence: each objective is satisfiable only by encoders that capture what is semantically stable about an image, not what differs between views.










NoteFine-Tuning





After SSL pretraining, the encoder is adapted to a specific task. Four strategies span the tradeoff between cost and performance. (See the ViT note for details on LoRA.)
Frozen encoder + linear probing. Only a linear classifier head is trained on top of the frozen backbone. This is the fastest option and a standard benchmark for representation quality: a good SSL representation should be linearly separable for most tasks.
Frozen encoder + nonlinear head. A small MLP head replaces the linear classifier, allowing more flexible adaptation without touching the backbone.
LoRA fine-tuning. The backbone is frozen; small low-rank update matrices are added to the attention projections and trained alongside the task head. This gives more flexibility than a fixed head while keeping trainable parameters below 1% of the backbone.
Full fine-tuning. All parameters are updated. Most effective when the target domain is distant from the pretraining distribution and when enough labelled data exists to avoid overfitting.










NotePractical Considerations





Augmentations. Standard natural-image augmentations (crops, color jitter, blur) often transfer to new domains without modification. For medical images, intensity normalization variants and orientation changes are worth adding; aggressive color jitter or grayscale may not apply depending on the modality.
Scale. SSL improves with both data scale and model scale. Diversity matters more than raw dataset size: a narrow distribution produces narrow representations. Among ViTs, ViT-L and larger consistently outperform ViT-B in downstream transfer when data allows.
Starting from a pretrained checkpoint. Training SSL from scratch is expensive and rarely necessary. Strong publicly available checkpoints (DINOv2, MAE-pretrained ViT-L) provide an excellent starting point for most domains.











NoteAppendix A: InfoNCE, Collapse, and Alignment vs. Uniformity












NoteInfoNCE





InfoNCE treats representation learning as a multi-class classification problem. Given a batch of \(N\) images, each with two augmented views, the loss over one positive pair \((z_i^{(1)}, z_i^{(2)})\) is:
\[
\mathcal{L}_i = -\log \frac{\exp\!\left(z_i^{(1)} \cdot z_i^{(2)}\,/\,\tau\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp\!\left(z_i^{(1)} \cdot z_j^{(2)}\,/\,\tau\right)}
\]
The \(j=i\) term in the denominator is the positive; all \(j \neq i\) terms are negatives drawn from the same batch. The denominator normalizes over all \(N\) candidates, so the model must score the true positive higher than every other image in the batch.
The temperature \(\tau\) controls sharpness. Low \(\tau\) concentrates gradients on the hardest negatives; high \(\tau\) distributes gradients more evenly. SimCLR uses \(\tau = 0.07\).
Minimizing InfoNCE is equivalent to maximizing a lower bound on the mutual information \(I(z^{(1)}; z^{(2)})\) between the two views.










NoteRepresentation Collapse





Representation collapse occurs when the encoder maps all inputs to the same point in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). A collapsed encoder minimizes any positive-pair similarity loss trivially, but its features carry no information.
Different methods prevent collapse in different ways.
Contrastive methods prevent collapse through negatives: a constant representation scores equally against all negatives, so it cannot minimize the InfoNCE denominator.
BYOL uses an asymmetric prediction head on the student side only. The asymmetry breaks the symmetry that would allow both networks to collapse simultaneously.
DINO uses two mechanisms: centering subtracts a running mean from the teacher output before softmax, preventing any single prototype dimension from dominating; sharpening applies a lower temperature to the teacher softmax, keeping the training target peaked rather than flat.
MAE prevents collapse by construction: pixel reconstruction has a non-trivial target that cannot be satisfied by a constant output.










NoteAlignment and Uniformity





SSL objectives can be decomposed into two complementary pressures.
Alignment measures how close positive pairs are:
\[
\mathcal{L}_\text{align} = \mathbb{E}_{(x,\, x^+) \sim p_\text{pos}} \left\|f(x) - f(x^+)\right\|^2
\]
Uniformity measures how evenly representations are spread across the unit hypersphere:
\[
\mathcal{L}_\text{uniform} = \log\; \mathbb{E}_{x,\,y \sim p_\text{data}} \left[\, e^{-2\|f(x) - f(y)\|^2} \,\right]
\]
A good representation minimizes both: positives are close (alignment), and the overall distribution does not collapse to a subspace (uniformity). InfoNCE optimizes both simultaneously: the numerator promotes alignment, and the denominator promotes uniformity by penalizing any representation that is close to many others. Self-distillation methods primarily optimize alignment; their collapse-prevention mechanisms serve as a proxy for uniformity.

title: Vision Transformers
Mutual Information
text:
Note1. Statistical dependence





Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are statistically dependent if observing \(X\) makes some values of \(Y\) more or less likely, or vice versa. Formally, this means that the conditional distribution differs from the marginal distribution, i.e. \(p(y \mid x) \neq p(y)\), for some values of \(x\) and \(y\).
Conversely, \(X\) and \(Y\) are statistically independent if and only if \(p(y \mid x) = p(y)\), for all \(x\) and \(y\). Using the chain rule of probability (\(p(x,y) = p(x)\,p(y \mid x)\)), this implies that the joint distribution factorizes as the product of marginals: \(p(x,y) = p(x)\,p(y)\).






NoteSummary




Statistical dependence: \(p(y \mid x) \neq p(y)\)
Statistical independence: \(p(y \mid x) = p(y)\)












Note2. Statistical dependence quantification - motivation





Statements like \(p(y \mid x) \neq p(y)\) or \(p(y \mid x) = p(y)\) tell us whether two variables are statistically dependent. In many machine learning problems, however, we are also interested in measuring (and often optimizing) the degree of statistical dependence between variables, i.e. how much observing one variable changes the distribution of the other.
For instance, in representation learning, we often want to learn features \(Z = f_\theta(X)\) from an input \(X\) such that \(Z\) is maximally statistically dependent on \(X\). Similarly, in multi-view or multimodal input setups, we have multiple measurements of the same underlying phenomenon, e.g. two augmented views of the same image, or images and text describing the same object. Here, \(X\) and \(Y\) are different measurements of the same latent source \(Z\) (e.g. the scene content or object identity). A common goal here is to learn representations \(Z_X = f_\theta(X), Z_Y = g_\phi(Y)\) such that the statistical dependence between \(Z_X\) and \(Z_Y\) is maximized.









Note3. Statistical dependence quantification via mutual information





Recall that statistical independence means \(p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)\). A natural way to measure the strength of dependence is therefore to compare the true joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) with the distribution that would arise under independence \(p(x)p(y)\).
First, for a particular sample pair \((x,y)\), we consider the ratio \(\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\), which compares how often \((x,y)\) occurs in reality to how often it would occur if the variables were independent. Second, we take the logarithm of this ratio. The quantity \(\log \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\) is sometimes called the pointwise mutual information of the pair \((x,y)\). Finally, we average over all outcomes, weighting each pair \((x,y)\) by how frequently it occurs. The resulting quantity is called the mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\):
\[\boxed{I(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)}\!\left[\log \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\right]}\]
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)\) and the ratio equals \(1\) everywhere, therefore \(I(X,Y) = 0\). If not, \(p(x,y) \neq p(x)p(y)\), and \(I(X,Y) > 0\). This follows from recognising that MI is a KL divergence (see appendix), which is always non-negative.









Note4. Mutual information as uncertainty reduction





Above, we introduced mutual information as a measure of the degree of statistical dependence between two random variables. Here, we present an alternative view: MI measures how much information one variable provides about another, or equivalently, how much uncertainty about one variable is reduced by knowing the other.
Probability distributions as a measure of uncertainty: A probability distribution over a random variable encodes our uncertainty about its value. It tells us which outcomes are likely and which are not. A distribution concentrated on a single value means we are near-certain, a spread-out or uniform distribution means we are highly uncertain. Entropy \(H(Y) = -\mathbb{E}[\log p(Y)]\) quantifies this average uncertainty as a single number: it is large when \(p(y)\) is diffuse and small when \(p(y)\) is peaked.
Statistical dependence implies uncertainty reduction: When \(X\) and \(Y\) are statistically dependent, observing \(X = x\) shifts the distribution over \(Y\) from \(p(y)\) to \(p(y \mid x)\), changing how uncertain we are about \(Y\). Conditional entropy \(H(Y \mid X) = -\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)}[\log p(y \mid x)]\) captures the remaining uncertainty about \(Y\) after observing \(X\), averaged over all possible values of \(X\).
MI as a measure of uncertainty reduction: Mutual information is the average reduction in uncertainty about \(Y\) due to observing \(X\): \(I(X, Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\). Substituting the definitions of MI, entropy, and conditional entropy confirms this identity.







NoteSummary



Three views of mutual information:

The strength of statistical dependence between two variables
The information one variable provides about the other
The reduction in uncertainty about one variable due to knowing the other




Units
The units of mutual information depend on the logarithm base (base \(2\) → bits, base \(e\) → nats). Using base \(2\), mutual information can be interpreted as the number of bits of uncertainty about one variable that are reduced on average by observing the other. For discrete variables, this has a concrete meaning: one bit corresponds to the answer to one fair yes/no question, so \(I(X,Y) = k\) bits means observing \(X\) saves you, on average, \(k\) binary questions about \(Y\). For continuous variables, this interpretation breaks down. MI can be unbounded and the absolute value in bits is not directly meaningful. It is better treated as a relative measure, where larger MI indicates stronger dependence.









Note5. Challenges in computing mutual information





The definition above assumes that we know the joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) and the marginal distributions \(p(x)\) and \(p(y)\). In practice, however, these distributions are rarely known and must be estimated from samples. This becomes particularly challenging in high dimensions. For example, if \(X\) and \(Y\) are images with thousands of pixels, the joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) lives in a space with thousands of dimensions. Accurately estimating such distributions from finite data quickly becomes infeasible. As a result, practical applications of mutual information typically rely on approximate estimators, lower-dimensional representations, or surrogate objectives. Three main families of approaches are used in practice:
Non-parametric estimators: Methods such as the KSG estimator compute MI directly from samples using \(k\)-nearest-neighbour distances in the joint space, without assuming a parametric form for the distributions. These are accurate in low dimensions but scale poorly as dimensionality grows.
Variational lower bounds: Methods such as MINE and InfoNCE parameterise a critic network and optimise a tractable lower bound on MI (see appendix). These scale to high-dimensional continuous variables but the bound can be loose, particularly when the true MI is large.
Proxy objectives: In many machine learning applications, MI maximisation is replaced with objectives that are easier to optimise and are known empirically to correlate with high MI. Contrastive losses are the most widely used, forming the basis of self-supervised methods such as SimCLR. These do not produce an estimate of the MI value but are computationally practical at scale.









NoteAppendix: MI as a KL divergence





The KL divergence from distribution \(q\) to distribution \(p\) is defined as:
\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) = \mathbb{E}_{p}\!\left[\log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right]\]
It measures how different \(p\) is from \(q\), and satisfies \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) \geq 0\), with equality if and only if \(p = q\).
Mutual information is exactly the KL divergence from the product of marginals \(p(x)p(y)\) to the joint \(p(x,y)\):
\[I(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)}\!\left[\log \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\right] = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(x,y) \,\|\, p(x)p(y))\]
Non-negativity of KL divergence therefore implies \(I(X,Y) \geq 0\), with equality if and only if \(p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)\), i.e. when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.









NoteAppendix: Variational lower bounds on MI





Because MI cannot be computed directly in high dimensions, a common strategy is to train a critic network \(T_\theta(x,y)\) to estimate the log pointwise MI ratio \(\log \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\) at every pair \((x,y)\). Once the critic is accurate, averaging its outputs over samples from the joint gives an estimate of MI. The critic is trained by contrasting positive pairs \((x,y) \sim p(x,y)\) (pairs that actually co-occur) against negative pairs \((x,y') \sim p(x)p(y)\) (independently sampled, so statistically independent by construction). MINE and InfoNCE differ in the loss used to learn this contrast.
